hypotheses.name: Nobody’s hurrying on Hormuz — HELD at 60%
hypotheses.d: The near-breakthrough-then-condition pattern fired a sixth time (Iran–Oman interim corridor and 30–60 days of technical talks, against Ghalibaf restating the full condition stack). Deliberately not moved: it is already priced, and a minesweeping calendar is what an honest process looks like too. The real test is live — the offer sits with the IRGC, so Tehran's answer is the experiment.

hypotheses.name: Détente as harvest cover — 55% → 60%
hypotheses.d: The discriminating split signal arrived: PLA sorties kept declining while the coast guard escalated in kind — CCG 2307 pressing a Japanese coast guard ship in the strait Aug 6–10, which AEI reads as testing whether foreign vessels will obey PRC authority. Kinetic down, jurisdiction up is the ratchet signature. Capped at +5; the stated tell is what the coast guard does through the Sept 24 visit.

hypotheses.name: NEW · Venezuela was a Hormuz hedge in a drug-war uniform
hypotheses.d: The clearest revealed-preference play on the board — and the reason it opens at 55 rather than higher. Sturdy mechanism first: US Gulf-Coast refineries are plumbed for heavy sour crude, Venezuela sits on the planet's largest heavy reserves, and moving that barrel north through the Caribbean to Texas and Louisiana structurally hedges the one risk that ran live all year — a Hormuz closure. The Aug 28-29 deal (a new operator taking control of ~65bn barrels, about a fifth of Venezuela's reserves) is exactly what this hypothesis predicts, and the reporting frames it in plain words as an alternative to Gulf oil routed through Hormuz. So oil-as-motive is near-certain. What is NOT settled — and what caps this — is premeditation: was Operation Southern Spear a counter-narcotics and regime-change campaign that harvested the oil after the fact, or an oil-security operation in a drug-war uniform from the start? The tell against design is the clock — the deal trailed Maduro's Jan 3 capture by eight months, which reads more like spoils than master plan. Mundane alternative, named and live: drugs, migration politics, regime-change, with the barrel a bonus. Falsifiers — cut hard if export volumes stay token (the $2-2.8bn tranches are a rounding error against control of 65bn bbl), if Gulf-Coast heavy sourcing does not actually swing off the Middle East, or if the fixed infrastructure (GEO-022) never appears. One correction the excitement needs: a canal cannot bypass Hormuz, geography does not work that way — the hedge is source substitution plus Caribbean routing, not a waterway. Real Orinoco or Maracaibo channel-dredging and dedicated heavy-crude terminals WOULD be the premeditation tell. Unconfirmed today; it is the thing to watch.

hypotheses.name: US drift hardened into leverage play — 45% → 52%
hypotheses.d: Economic Outcast hit ~60 teapots, tankers and traders and touched no Chinese state major and no bank — Treasury sent the majors a warning letter instead. Maximum pressure on Iran, calibrated to stop exactly short of anything that would detonate the Sept 24 summit. Held to +7 because the Munir offer is a real concession, and $4.10 gas before midterms is real evidence against premeditation.

hypotheses.name: NEW · A pre-announcement leak into oil futures
hypotheses.d: Four times in the war window, nine- and ten-figure short bets landed 15–20 minutes before an Iran announcement: ~$2.2bn across crude, gasoil and gasoline before Trump's Mar 23 pause post; ~$950m before the Apr 7 ceasefire; ~$760m before Iran said Hormuz would open. ~$7bn total; CFTC probing, four members of Congress demanding answers. Split: deliberate leak 45 / mediator-side 20 / skilled opportunism 25 / coincidence 10. This is the only entry in the book whose evidence is timestamped BEFORE the event rather than pattern-matched after — which is why it opens this high. Against it: no episode has surfaced around this week's diplomacy.

hypotheses.name: Moscow shapes Tehran's maximalism — 30% → 25%
hypotheses.d: Cut again. The channels that actually moved this week were Oman, Pakistan and the new Mecca defence pact — Russia was absent from every one of them, and still has not offered the mediation this hypothesis expects. Motive 9/10, documentary evidence 0/10, pre-event evidence never. Cut to 15% if nothing surfaces by Sept 30.

hypotheses.d: Both its live predictions came in favourably this week and it gets credit for neither: the rival leverage hypothesis predicted the same things, and shared predictions are ambience. One more failed pre-summit call and it goes to the epitaph list.

brief.h: The White House put terms on the Venezuela oil deal: the Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital takes a 35 percent stake in the private venture handed 100-year rights to 17 fields, and Washington gets to buy a fifth of the output at cost
brief.t: Follow the instrument, not the barrel. What was announced on Friday as the biggest oil deal in history is, in its published terms, a defence ministry buying equity in a foreign oil company - the Office of Strategic Capital, a Pentagon financing desk whose statutory tools are loans and guarantees, holding 35 percent of North American Blue Energy Partners, with a right routed through State to purchase 20 percent of output at cost for the strategic reserve and the military. Venezuela's interim president Delcy Rodriguez granted the venture 100-year rights over 17 fields holding 65 billion barrels of proven reserves, fields the White House points out were previously operated by Russian and Chinese firms, and the operator has committed $100bn of new infrastructure investment. The money question is who pays for the part that makes barrels move: Orinoco extra-heavy crude does not flow to a Gulf Coast coker without upgraders, diluent, power and channel depth, none of which exist at the claimed scale. Trump's own answer on when drivers would feel it - if it was two years, you know, that's a short period of time - is the honest timeline, and it is why this is a strategic position rather than a pump-price policy.
brief.context: R0, date the rail. This is a late chapter of the 1971-2022 epoch in which the United States stopped being able to guarantee its fuel with its own geology and started guaranteeing it with legal and financial instruments instead - and the specific instrument here is much older than that, going back to Churchill's 1914 purchase of 51 percent of Anglo-Persian for the Royal Navy. The desk that decides is not the podium and not even State: it is the Office of Strategic Capital, because a financing desk is the entity that can award the loans and guarantees that fixed export infrastructure requires, and its existence in the cap table is the change from Friday's announcement to today's terms. The mechanism to watch is source substitution, not routing - a canal cannot bypass Hormuz, geography does not permit it, so the hedge is that Gulf Coast refiners plumbed for heavy sour crude get their barrel from the Caribbean instead of from the Gulf. Base rate is the discipline here: state equity positions in foreign upstream convert into awarded fixed export logistics inside twelve months well under half the time, because permitting, sanctions carve-outs and political reversal all sit in the path. The influence map is unusually legible - principal, US Gulf refiners and the SPR; agent, a Pentagon financing office; narrator, an energy-price story before a midterm; operator, one Venezuelan businessman holding operatorship; target, a future elected Venezuelan government that inherits a contract it did not sign, and Canadian heavy producers whose discount widens if the barrels actually arrive. The falsifier is concrete: an awarded, funded dredging contract or a dedicated heavy-crude terminal tender within eighteen months confirms a pre-built rail; eighteen months of equity with no logistics award means this was a fee extracted from a client government, and the premeditation read should be marked down.

angles.effect: Gets an energy-security story and a below-market SPR refill before the midterms, bought with an announcement and a balance-sheet position rather than an appropriation - the cheapest available instrument

angles.party: The Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital
angles.effect: Acquires a permanent claim on a strategic commodity, and with it a permanent obligation to care who governs Caracas
Converts a transitional mandate into recognition, sanctions relief and $100bn of promised capital, paid for by pre-committing a century of the country's principal asset

angles.party: Future Venezuelan governments and Canadian heavy producers
angles.effect: Carry the bill - one inherits an unratified century-long concession, the other watches its heavy discount widen if the barrels actually reach the Gulf

dec.kill: A published contract text naming a governing law, an arbitration seat and the sanctions authorisation, followed within eighteen months by an awarded dredging or terminal contract, would confirm this is a durable supply rail. No published instrument and no logistics award by March 2028 means it was a headline with a lease number attached.

brief.h: Trump summoned Valero, Marathon, PBF and Chevron to the White House today with gasoline above $4 a gallon and diesel near $6 - the highest seasonal fuel prices ever recorded in the United States
brief.t: This is the domestic invoice for the strait, arriving at the desk that cannot pay it. Pump prices have gone from roughly $3 before Operation Epic Fury to above $4, and diesel - the fuel that prices freight, farming and therefore groceries - is close to $6, which is why eight in ten Americans tell pollsters the Iran campaign raised their cost of living. The meeting is billed as being about supply and capacity expansion, and that framing is where the analysis has to be done: US refining capacity is a multi-year construction problem and nothing agreed in a room today adds a barrel of throughput before November. What a president can actually deliver on this clock is regulatory - a federal gasoline-tax suspension, a summer-blend or renewable-obligation waiver, a product release from the reserve - and those are the instruments to watch for, because they are the tell that the administration has stopped expecting the price to fall on its own.
brief.context: Constraint before character. The binding constraint on the Iran file is not ideology, it is a calendar: 3 November, with pump prices above $4 and approval in the mid-30s. Run the plumbing lens and the mechanism is refining configuration, not crude supply - US Gulf Coast refineries are built to crack heavy sour barrels, the war removed the cheapest source of those barrels, and a refinery running an unfavourable slate produces less diesel per barrel, which is why the diesel number is worse than the gasoline number and why the diesel number is the one that reaches the grocery aisle. That is also the through-line to the Venezuela deal announced the same week: the two stories are one policy, an attempt to fix the input slate rather than the crude price. The base rate is unkind to the meeting - price-jawboning summits with refiners have a long record of producing letters and no measurable change in the retail spread, because refining margins are set by crack spreads in a global product market, not by presidential displeasure. The influence map runs principal, the midterm coalition; agent, the White House; operator, four refiners who control the throughput; market, the crack spread; target, drivers and freight. The falsifier is dated and cheap to check: if a gasoline-tax suspension or a blend waiver is announced within thirty days, the administration has conceded it cannot move the source price and is buying time; if nothing regulatory appears and the meeting produces only capacity language, it was theatre and the pump price stays a pure function of the strait.

angles.effect: Gains a visible act of doing something about prices, and a place to put the blame if they stay high
Gain leverage to ask for permitting and blend-rule relief they have wanted for years, in exchange for capacity promises that mature long after the election
Pay now. Diesel near $6 is a tax on every mile of every good moved, and it arrives in food prices with a lag rather than at the pump
Strengthens quietly - every week the domestic price of holding out is visible at cabinet level is a week the other side's patience is worth more

dec.kill: A gasoline-tax suspension, blend waiver or SPR product release inside thirty days confirms the administration has stopped expecting the source price to fall. Nothing regulatory and no measurable change in the retail spread by October means the meeting was a message to voters, not to molecules.

brief.h: The Permanent Court of Arbitration ruled unanimously that the Indus Waters Treaty remains fully in force and India had no valid ground to suspend it - and New Delhi replied that the court is illegally constituted and has zero legal standing
brief.t: A treaty that survived four wars has just been tested against a tribunal with no enforcement arm, and the tribunal lost. The five-member panel found the 1960 treaty remains binding, that India must observe its obligations on the design and operation of hydropower projects on the western rivers, and - acting on a Pakistani application - barred India from pouring concrete beyond a specified level at a Kashmir hydroelectric plant until 90 days after a World Bank-appointed neutral expert rules on the design. India has never recognised the body, never appeared, and said the same day that its April 2025 decision to hold the treaty in abeyance stands. Follow the physical asset rather than the legal one: India is the upstream state on rivers that irrigate roughly 80 percent of Pakistan's farmland, and upstream position is only leverage to the extent that storage and diversion capacity exists to use it, which is exactly what the disputed run-of-river projects incrementally build.
brief.context: The rail here predates every headline by 66 years: the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty, brokered and guaranteed by the World Bank, which allocated the three eastern rivers to India and the three western rivers to Pakistan and built a dispute mechanism - Permanent Indus Commission, then neutral expert, then court of arbitration - precisely because the drafters expected the parties to stop talking. The desk that decides is not the tribunal and not the foreign ministry; it is India's Ministry of Jal Shakti and the National Hydroelectric Power Corporation, because what changes the water balance is reservoir capacity and drawdown flushing schedules, not awards. The mechanism is Schelling's salami tactic applied to hydrology: no single run-of-river project deprives Pakistan of water, but each one adds storage and timing control, and timing control on a monsoon-dependent irrigation system during the sowing window is the coercive asset. Base rate: states that formally deny an arbitral body's jurisdiction and refuse to appear comply with the resulting award only rarely, and almost never inside a year - which is why the new GEO-024 opens at 12 percent on restoration rather than at a number that flatters international law. The influence map is short and that is what makes it dangerous - principal, Indian domestic politics after the 2025 Pahalgam attack; agent, New Delhi; operator, dam engineers; target, Punjabi and Sindhi farmers with no vote in Delhi; and no narrator, because water disputes get almost no coverage until they are a crisis. Falsifier: India resuming Permanent Indus Commission participation or publicly restoring the treaty would mean the abeyance was a bargaining posture; concrete poured past the prohibited level, or a new western-river project announced, would mean the legal rail is being replaced by a physical one.

angles.effect: Gains a durable coercive instrument over its rival's food system and a domestic political win, at the cost of its own standing as a rules-based power in every other forum it wants to be taken seriously in
Gains a unanimous legal victory it cannot enforce, and a talking point that costs Islamabad nothing and buys it nothing
Pays the reputational bill as the treaty's guarantor with no coercive instrument - and every future water treaty it brokers is priced against this precedent
Carry the actual risk. They are the ones for whom a shifted release schedule during a sowing window is not a legal question

dec.kill: India resuming Permanent Indus Commission meetings or publicly restoring the treaty would show the abeyance was posture. Concrete poured past the prohibited level at Kishanganga or Ratle, or a new run-of-river announcement on the western rivers, would show the legal rail is being replaced by a physical one.

brief.h: Pezeshkian said Iran would return to the June memorandum immediately if Washington does, and Qatar said it would intensify mediation - hours after Trump called this a relatively little war and said the US would hit Iran hard
brief.t: Weigh the offer by who made it, not by what it says. Iran's elected president saying Tehran would take reciprocal action immediately is the seventh instance this ledger has counted of a near-breakthrough announcement that arrives with a condition attached and no unconditional step behind it, and it comes from the branch of the Iranian state that has been overridden on this exact file three times since April - the April truce, the June memorandum re-closed in three days, and the July talks killed by vessel strikes. The desk that decides Hormuz is the IRGC Navy, which announced the weekend's missile volleys, and which answered a US strike on its minelayers within hours. Meanwhile the price is doing the negotiating: Brent above $92 for a second day, up roughly 30 percent on pre-war levels, is the market voting on how much of this offer it believes.
brief.context: The permit regime is the rail. Iran's leverage at Hormuz was never over the water - it is over the insurance and routing cost of using it, administered through the Persian Gulf Strait Authority the IRGC stood up during the war, which is an institution with rents attached rather than a chip a foreign ministry can trade. That is why this board's conditional forecast that any deal preserves Iranian transit-administration machinery sits at 76 percent. The mechanism to watch is actuarial, not diplomatic: reopening is decided by war-risk underwriters at the Joint War Committee pricing incident frequency in a specific lane over a specific quiet period, and two hulls struck inside the corridor Washington declared cleared on 28 August resets that clock no matter what any president offers. Base rate comes from the Tanker War of 1984-88, where traffic recovered only after a ceasefire plus convoying and never during an attack series. Fortna's finding is the anchor on the settlement side: ceasefires with an agreed third-party verifier hold materially better, and this framework has none - Qatar mediating is not the same object as an inspection regime with a name. The influence map: principal, an IRGC whose institutional power IS the permit regime; agent, a presidency that keeps making offers it cannot deliver; narrator, Qatari and Omani mediation; operator, minelayers and underwriters; target, Asian refiners and American drivers. Falsifier, dated and already published: no attack on a laden tanker in the international lanes through 22 September plus a published minesweeping calendar out of Muscat scores our recurrence read a MISS rather than deferring it.

angles.effect: Gains standing as the reasonable party at zero cost, since the offer is conditional on a US move and can be withdrawn by an institution he does not control
Loses nothing. An offer it has overridden three times does not bind it, and the permit regime that is its institutional property is not on the table in any version of this
Faces the harder choice - accepting means visibly returning to a framework it walked away from, weeks before a midterm, which is the concession the coalition-capture hypothesis says it cannot make
Pay the spread either way. War-risk premia respond to incident counts, not to presidential statements, so a verbal offer moves their costs by roughly nothing

dec.kill: An unconditional Iranian step - published corridor coordinates, a minesweeping calendar, a widened permit schedule - would break the near-breakthrough-then-condition pattern and force this read up sharply. Another cycle ending in a restated condition makes it the seventh instance and confirms it.

brief.h: The bond rout deepened with Japan's 10-year at 3 percent for the first time since 1996 - and the leg nobody is pricing is supply, with US debt past $40 trillion and hyperscalers issuing into the same market to fund data centres Texas has just stopped connecting
brief.t: Yesterday's read on this tape was demand-side: an energy shock plus deficits nobody is consolidating. Today's reporting adds the other blade of the scissors, and it is the more interesting one. Governments are not the only borrowers crowding the long end - the AI buildout is being financed with bond issuance at a scale that competes with sovereign supply, and that private capex is now colliding with a physical constraint. Texas, the fastest-growing data-centre market on earth, has frozen new grid connections after interconnection requests exploded from about 48 gigawatts in 2023 to more than 474, a number ERCOT and the governor's office suspect is largely ghost demand - the same project counted at five utilities, or inquiries with no signed contract. Pennsylvania has followed with stricter permitting. If a material share of that pipeline is phantom, some of the debt raised against it is funding capacity that will never be energised, which is a credit question arriving in a market already repricing duration.
brief.context: Date the rail: this is the late chapter of the 1971-2022 epoch of ever-cheaper duration, and the specific subsidy that is ending is the yen. For thirty years near-zero Japanese funding was the shock absorber under everyone else's long end - Japanese institutions reached abroad for yield they could not get at home - and at a 3 percent JGB that forced march reverses and the money comes home. The desk that decides is not a central bank podium: it is the primary dealers who have to underwrite each auction, which is why a tailed or failed JGB or gilt auction is the tripwire rather than any policy statement. The mechanism worth naming is crowding-out in its literal form - a fixed pool of duration buyers facing sovereign issuance from a $40tn debt stock plus corporate issuance from a capex boom, with the marginal buyer setting the price for both. The base rate is the guardrail: most yield spikes are energy scares that retrace when the barrel does, and term-premium regime shifts are roughly generational events, so the prior should be on fizzle. On the ghost-demand question specifically, the honest analogue is the late-1990s fibre buildout, where enormous capacity was financed against demand forecasts that were real in direction and wildly wrong in magnitude, and the reckoning arrived in credit rather than in technology. Falsifier: long yields in three G7 countries retreating 50 basis points before December while the Middle East file stays open scores this an inflation scare, and the structural reading is marked down rather than deferred.

angles.effect: Gain first-mover position on scarce grid capacity by filing interconnection requests everywhere - which is individually rational and collectively produces exactly the phantom number regulators are now investigating
Pay if the buildout is oversized. Transmission built against ghost demand lands in the rate base, and residential customers cover it for decades
Pay the crowding-out cost. Every dollar of AI capex issuance competes for the same duration buyers that have to absorb a $40tn debt stock
Gain leverage and information by pausing - the freeze is cheap for them and expensive for anyone whose financing assumed a queue position

dec.kill: If interconnection queues survive the Texas audit largely intact and signed contracts back most of the 474 gigawatts, the ghost-demand read is wrong and this is a genuine supply shock in power. If the reviewed queue collapses by more than half, the credit question is real and it will show up in spreads before it shows up in a data centre.

lesson: In June 1914, weeks before the war, Winston Churchill stood up in the Commons as First Lord of the Admiralty and asked Parliament to buy 51 percent of the Anglo-Persian Oil Company. The argument was not commercial. He had converted the Royal Navy from Welsh coal to oil for speed, and in doing so had made the fleet dependent on a liquid Britain did not produce - so the state bought the producer rather than trust the market to sell to it in a crisis. That is the rail under today's Venezuela announcement, and it is worth naming precisely: a defence ministry taking an equity position in a foreign oil venture is not an investment, it is a supply guarantee bought with a balance sheet instead of a contract, and it appears whenever a military finds its fuel on the far side of somebody else's chokepoint. The Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital holding 35 percent of a Venezuelan venture, with a right to buy a fifth of the output at cost for the reserve and the military, is Churchill's instrument with the serial numbers filed off. What the precedent predicts is the part nobody announces on day one. State equity creates a state obligation to defend the asset, and it converts every subsequent local political change into a foreign-policy problem: APOC's stake bought Britain fuel for two wars and then bought it Mossadegh's nationalisation in 1951 and a coup in 1953, because a century-long claim on another country's principal resource outlives the government that granted it. So here is the falsifiable version rather than the cautionary tale. If this is a supply guarantee in the Churchill mould, the fixed infrastructure follows the equity - awarded dredging, a dedicated heavy-crude terminal, upgraders - because barrels you own but cannot move are not a guarantee; if eighteen months pass with the stake in place and no funded logistics award, then this was a fee extracted from a client government rather than a rail, and the analogy should be marked down accordingly.

lecture.title: The Economic Weapon: Why Sieges Make the Wars They Mean to Prevent

sections.t: Treasury designated roughly sixty Chinese “teapot” refiners — the small plants buying discounted Iranian crude — while touching no Chinese state major and no bank. The same week, central banks bought a record 288.9 tonnes of gold in the quarter gold fell over 20%. Two stories, one machine.

sections.h: Follow the money, name the mechanism
sections.t: A reserve manager buying into a 20% drawdown is not trading. He is hedging ACCESS — the risk that an asset held abroad gets switched off by its host government — and gold is the only large reserve asset with no counterparty who can flip that switch. Name the mechanism: the ECONOMIC WEAPON, using the financial plumbing whose hubs one country owns to inflict a siege without laying one. Iran discounts crude to Chinese teapots paying through dollar-touching chains; Treasury designates them; the IRGC's Strait Authority recoups the shortfall in Hormuz tolls. Sanction and gold bar are one transaction seen from two ends.

sections.h: Deep history I — the blockade that became an idea
sections.t: The economic weapon has a birthday and a founding failure. The birthday is November 1806, when Napoleon's Berlin Decrees declared the British Isles blockaded — the Continental System, an attempt to beat a maritime power by closing a continent's markets to it. It succeeded at nothing except generating enforcement. Portugal would not comply, so France invaded in 1807 and got the Peninsular War, the ulcer that bled the Grande Armée for six years. Alexander I quit the system in December 1810 because it was ruining Russian trade, and in 1812 Napoleon marched east to enforce it. The blockade never defeated Britain; it manufactured the two wars that destroyed the blockader. Sanctions require enforcement, and enforcement against a determined leakage path tends toward conquest. The second case mattered because it worked. The Allied blockade of Germany ran from 1914 through the armistice and was lifted only when Germany signed at Versailles in June 1919. German official estimates put civilian deaths from malnutrition near 424,000 — contested, and historians still argue how much was blockade and how much German agricultural mismanagement. But perception makes policy, and a generation concluded hunger had beaten an undefeated army. So they institutionalized it as a PEACE instrument: Article 16 of the League Covenant made sanctions automatic against an aggressor, and Wilson in 1919 put it in words no Treasury official would dare use today — “A nation that is boycotted is a nation that is in sight of surrender. Apply this economic, peaceful, silent, deadly remedy and there will be no need for force.” The weapon was invented to ABOLISH war; the rest of the century refutes that sentence.

sections.h: Deep history II — the failures that define our problem
sections.t: ABYSSINIA, 1935. Italy invaded Ethiopia; the League invoked Article 16 — exempting oil, coal and steel, and never closing the Suez Canal, which Britain controlled and through which Italian troopships sailed. Mussolini won anyway. The sanctions were real enough to enrage and too porous to stop, and the lesson is sharper than “sanctions don't work”: a sanction calibrated to spare the sender teaches the target that the sender is deterred too. Then the second-order effect. Nicholas Mulder's argument in The Economic Weapon is that the interwar regime deterred small states and PROVOKED large ones. Italy, Germany and Japan drew the same conclusion from the 1930s — dependence on seaborne trade was a vulnerability an enemy could switch off at will, and the answer was autarky, self-sufficiency taken by force. Lebensraum and the Co-Prosperity Sphere were ideological projects; they were also sanctions-proofing programs. Japan is the proof case. Washington embargoed scrap iron in 1940, then froze Japanese assets on 26 July 1941; America supplied roughly 80% of Japan's oil, and with Britain and the Dutch East Indies following, Japan lost about 88% of its oil imports. Reserves would last three years at peace, half that at war — Nagano's image was of a patient wasting away, every month of compliance leaving Japan weaker against the enemy it expected to fight. Pearl Harbor came in December. And the detail that turns story into discipline: the freeze was never meant to be total. Roosevelt intended a licensing regime keeping oil flowing so the tap stayed usable as leverage; officials in State and Treasury administered it so strictly that no licences issued and the flow stopped. The sanction that helped produce Pearl Harbor was substantially an organizational outcome, not a presidential decision — Allison's Essence of Decision, live. Before inferring “Iran's strategy” from one action, ask which bureau took it.

sections.h: The pattern — and where it breaks
sections.t: The leakage path is always the whole story — not the designation list, the leak: Portugal and Russia in 1806, Beira and Pretoria in 1966, Chinese teapots now. NOW THE BREAK. Japan in 1941 had a military option that promised to SOLVE its resource problem: seize the Dutch East Indies and own the oil. Iran has none — it fought its war, lost the conventional exchange, and has played its asymmetric card, the Hormuz toll. Nor did 1914 face an alternative supplier: Iran's is the world's second-largest economy, which the sanctioner just spared. Less Pearl Harbor, more Rhodesia.

MULDER says the siege provokes: strangulation drives large states to autarky, then preemption. DREZNER says sanctions are cheap theater — Hufbauer's data give a third success rate at best, near zero against great powers. The 2026 evidence buries neither: it splits by SIDE, and the split is the finding. On the TARGET Mulder scores: gold, stockpiles, payment rails, enrichment acceleration under maximum pressure. On the SENDER Drezner scores harder — the carve-outs. Sixty teapots and not one bank is not escalation; it is the sanctioner taking its own threat hostage, because hitting a Chinese bank endangers the dollar system that makes the hammer heavy.

The 2015 architecture is not coming back (high confidence): the 2022 freeze of Russian reserves turned the settlement network into an instrument; a hedge once bought is not resold. Expect bifurcation, not de-dollarization (moderate-high). EICHENGREEN is right that currencies erode glacially; the WEAPON depreciates faster than the CURRENCY. The bolder call (moderate): the most dangerous decade is the one in which the weapon still works but no longer terrifies. Mulder's mechanism fires in the transition — invested in escaping, not finished, expecting strangulation regardless. For China, the 2030s — so Economic D-Day may SHORTEN the fuse it was meant to lengthen. FALSIFIER: designate a major Chinese state bank; if Beijing cuts Iranian purchases within a quarter, I am wrong. Two centuries say the economic weapon does not replace war — it sorts the world into blocs that survive each other's sieges, then gives the survivors a reason to fight.

Nicholas Mulder, The Economic Weapon (2022) — published weeks before the Russia sanctions matched its template. Farrell & Newman, “Weaponized Interdependence” (2019) — it called the 2022 playbook and the chip controls in advance. Eichengreen, Exorbitant Privilege — the counterweight.

A century-long concession with no published instrument is a press release with a lease number attached

Whether anything with a dredge or a jetty in it appears - an awarded Orinoco or Maracaibo channel contract, a dedicated heavy-crude terminal tender. That is the premeditation tell GEO-022 scores, and it is the difference between spoils and design

Whether the refiner meeting produces an instrument or an announcement: a gasoline-tax suspension, a blend or RVO waiver, an SPR product release. Refining capacity cannot be added before November, so anything real will be regulatory

Whether the long-end repricing has a second act: a tailed JGB or gilt auction, a Bank of Japan statement on the 30-year, or a hyperscaler bond deal that prices materially wide of talk
Whether an American is killed or a US-flagged hull is struck - still the sharpest open trigger on the board, and still unfired
